data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001's central mechanistic claim that a shared checklist induces PERFECTLY correlated errors across non-experts is empirically false. Training and applying the same rules does not guarantee identical interpretations or execution. Within a single evaluation, panels of trained non-experts frequently show measurable inter-rater disagreement in scoring, boundary coding, or ambiguous item interpretation. If panelists apply the checklist with even stochastic variability, the effective n > 1, so aggregation can still reduce random noise independent of checklist bias. SRC_001 concedes this possibility in its counterconditions but its main claim and mechanism treat the correlation as perfect, which overstates the case and fails to account for the reliability gain the problem asks it to address.
